four_pillars.description: Baalorlord's four fundamental pillars that every successful deck must address. A deck that is weak in any pillar will struggle. Evaluate your deck against these pillars after every card reward and shop visit.

damage_output.description: Your ability to deal damage to enemies. Split into two sub-categories: frontloaded damage and scaling damage. You need BOTH — frontloaded for hallway fights and early turns, scaling for long boss fights.

frontload.description: Damage you can deal in the first 1-2 turns of combat without any setup. This is your bread and butter for hallway fights and the early turns of elite/boss fights.
frontload.importance: Critical in Act 1 where you have no scaling yet. Hallway fights should ideally end in 2-3 turns. If fights drag on, you take unnecessary damage that limits your pathing options.
frontload.target: Aim to deal 30-40+ damage in the first 2 turns by mid-Act 1. By Act 2, you want 50+ frontloaded damage available.
examples: Silent: Backstab, Predator, Dash, Poisoned Stab
Defect: Cold Snap, Ball Lightning, Doom and Gloom, Compile Driver
Necrobinder: Osty attacks, Doom application cards
Regent: Sovereign Blade (with Forge stacks), Star-powered attacks
frontload.common_mistake: Ignoring frontload in favor of scaling. A deck full of scaling cards with no frontload will lose 30+ HP in hallway fights before the scaling comes online.

scaling.description: Damage that grows over the course of a fight. Strength, Poison stacks, Focus + Orbs, Doom accumulation, Forge stacks — anything that makes each subsequent turn deal more damage than the last.
scaling.importance: Essential for boss fights and tough elites that last 5+ turns. Without scaling, bosses become wars of attrition you will lose. The longer a fight goes, the more scaling matters.
scaling.target: Have at least one reliable scaling source by the end of Act 1. By Act 2, you want 2+ scaling sources or one very strong one.
examples: Ironclad: Demon Form, Inflame, Spot Weakness, Limit Break
Defect: Defragment, Biased Cognition, Capacitor, Echo Form
Regent: Star generation engines, Forge accumulation
scaling.common_mistake: Over-investing in scaling without enough block or frontload. A Demon Form is worthless if you die on turn 2.

cycle_time.description: How quickly you see your important cards again. Cycle time is determined by deck size, draw, and card manipulation. A smaller, tighter deck with good draw sees its power cards every 2 turns instead of every 4.
cycle_time.ideal_deck_size: 20-25 cards for most builds. Some exhaust-heavy builds can go larger (28-32) because they thin in combat. Some ultra-thin builds work at 15-18 but require specific synergies.
cycle_time.target_cycle: See your full deck every ~2 turns. With a 20-card deck and 5-card hand, you see everything in 4 draws (2 turns). Add draw cards and it's even faster.
cycle_time.why_it_matters: If your deck has 35 cards and your win condition is 3 specific cards, you might not see them together for 5+ turns. That's 5 turns of taking damage without your engine running.
tips: Skip card rewards more often than you take them — every card you add increases cycle time
Prioritize draw cards: they effectively reduce your deck size by letting you see more cards per turn
Remove Strikes and Defends at every opportunity — they are the weakest cards in your deck
Exhaust cards naturally thin your deck during combat, improving cycle time as the fight progresses
Innate cards reduce effective cycle time by guaranteeing key cards in opening hand
Retain cards improve consistency by letting you hold key cards across turns
card_removal_priority: Strikes first (they deal less damage than almost any common attack)
Defends second (they block less than almost any common skill)

block_density.description: The percentage of your deck that can generate block. You need enough block cards to survive enemy attacks on most turns, but not so many that you can't kill enemies.
block_density.target_description: Roughly 1 in 3 cards should generate block. In a 21-card deck, that's ~7 block cards. This ensures you draw at least 1-2 block cards per hand.
tips: Block cards that also do something else (Shrug It Off draws, Dash blocks AND attacks) are premium picks
Don't neglect block in Act 1 — you need to survive elites and the Act 1 boss
Strength/scaling builds still need block; you can't just race bosses
Artifact and Intangible are the best 'block' in the game — they prevent damage entirely
Calculate how much incoming damage you expect and whether your block density can handle it
Dexterity increases the value of every block card — it's block scaling

scaling_block.description: Block that grows over time, similar to damage scaling. Dexterity, Metallicize, After Image, Frost Orbs with Focus — these make your block better every turn.
examples: Ironclad: Barricade + Body Slam, Metallicize, Feel No Pain
Defect: Frost Orbs + Focus, Glacier, Reinforced Body
Necrobinder: Osty as meat shield, defensive Souls

upgrade_density.description: The percentage of your deck that is upgraded. Upgraded cards are significantly more efficient — they deal more damage, block more, cost less, or gain additional effects. Campfires are your primary upgrade source.
upgrade_density.target_description: Aim to have at least half your deck upgraded by Act 2. By Act 3, 60-75% upgraded is ideal. Upgrades are one of the most reliable ways to increase deck power.
tips: Upgrading is almost always better than resting at a campfire if you're above 50% HP
Prioritize upgrading your most-played cards — cards you see every fight benefit most from upgrades
Some upgrades are transformative: Bash+ applies 3 Vulnerable, Neutralize+ applies 2 Weak, etc.
Calculate the total value of an upgrade over an entire run — an upgraded card played 50+ times adds up enormously
Key upgrades that change card function (add draw, reduce cost, add effects) are highest priority
Upgrades to 0-cost cards are often very efficient since you always play them
upgrade_priority_framework: 1. Cards that gain new effects when upgraded (cost reduction, added draw, new mechanics)
2. Cards you play every single turn (your most consistent damage/block sources)
3. Scaling cards (making your scaling faster or stronger compounds over a fight)
4. Cards that go from situational to always-good when upgraded
5. Cards with minor stat bumps (last priority — +3 damage is less impactful than a new effect)

card_evaluation.description: How to evaluate card rewards and decide what to take, skip, or remove.

jobs_framework.description: Baalorlord's 'Jobs' framework for card evaluation. Every card should fill a specific job your deck needs. Don't evaluate cards in a vacuum — evaluate them based on what your deck is currently missing.

jobs.when_needed: Always needed in Act 1. Check if your first 2 turns deal enough damage to kill small hallway enemies.

jobs.description: Grow damage output over a long fight
jobs.when_needed: Needed before first elite, critical before first boss. If you have no scaling, prioritize this.
Always needed. If less than ~30% of your deck generates block, prioritize block cards.

jobs.description: See more cards per turn, improve consistency
jobs.when_needed: Needed once deck size exceeds 20 cards. Critical if you have powerful cards you rarely see.
Need at least 1 AOE source by mid-Act 1. Multiple enemy fights are common and dangerous.

jobs.description: Weak, Vulnerable, or other debuffs that reduce enemy effectiveness
jobs.when_needed: Weak is always valuable (reduces damage by 25%). Vulnerable amplifies your damage by 50%.

jobs.description: Scry, retain, search, or otherwise control what you draw
jobs.when_needed: Becomes important in Act 2+ as fights become more complex and sequencing matters more.

evaluation_process: 1. Identify which jobs your deck currently needs most urgently
2. Evaluate each card reward by which job(s) it fills
3. Prefer cards that fill multiple jobs simultaneously (e.g., Shrug It Off blocks AND draws)
4. Skip the reward if no card fills a needed job — adding bloat is worse than skipping
5. Consider the next 3-5 fights: what do you need to survive RIGHT NOW?

two_cost_cards.description: Baalorlord emphasizes that new players chronically undervalue 2-cost cards. A 2-cost card that does 2 things is often more efficient than playing two 1-cost cards that each do one thing.
two_cost_cards.reasoning: A 2-cost card takes 1 card slot in your hand and 1 draw to see. Two 1-cost cards take 2 slots and 2 draws. The 2-cost card is better for cycle time even if the raw numbers seem similar.
examples: Carnage (2 cost, 20 damage) vs two Strikes (2 cost total, 12 damage) — Carnage wins on damage AND cycle time
Dash (2 cost, 10 damage + 10 block) replaces a Strike AND a Defend in one card slot
Doom and Gloom (2 cost, 10 damage + channel Dark orb) provides damage AND orb value in one play
when_to_avoid_two_cost: When you have very limited energy (3 energy with no energy relics)
When the 2-cost card's effect is too situational or conditional
When you already have too many 2-cost cards and can't play your full hand

skipping_philosophy.description: One of Baalorlord's most important teachings: skipping card rewards is a powerful strategic tool. Most players take too many cards.
key_principles: Every card you add to your deck increases cycle time — make sure it's worth it
A mediocre card is WORSE than no card because it dilutes your draws
In Act 2 and Act 3, you should be skipping 40-60% of card rewards
Ask yourself: 'Does this card make my deck better, or just bigger?'
The best players skip aggressively and have tight, focused decks
It's better to have a 20-card deck where every card is good than a 30-card deck with 10 filler cards
when_to_take: The card fills an urgent job your deck needs
The card has exceptional synergy with your existing cards
You're in Act 1 and need any reasonable damage or block
The card is a rare/powerful card you'd build around
when_to_skip: No card fills an urgent need
The cards are marginal upgrades over what you already have
Your deck is already 25+ cards and you don't have exhaust mechanics
Taking the card would reduce your consistency more than it adds power

hp_as_resource.description: Baalorlord's core teaching: HP is a resource to be SPENT, not hoarded. Taking 5 damage in a hallway fight to end it 1 turn faster is often correct because it saves you from taking 10 damage over 2 additional turns.
key_principles: HP is a resource, not a score — spending HP efficiently is a skill
Taking damage to end fights faster is often correct (less total damage taken)
Low HP forces bad pathing — maintaining 50%+ HP gives you options
Resting at campfires is almost always wrong if you're above 50% HP — upgrade instead
Elite fights are worth the HP investment if you can afford it — the rewards are massive

hp_thresholds.comfortable: 70%+ HP — take any fight, hunt elites freely
hp_thresholds.moderate: 50-70% HP — still take elites if your deck is strong, otherwise play safe
hp_thresholds.danger: 30-50% HP — avoid elites, consider resting at campfires
hp_thresholds.critical: Below 30% HP — rest at every campfire, take safest possible path, use potions liberally

potion_usage.description: Baalorlord strongly advocates using potions aggressively, especially on elites. Hoarding potions for the boss is one of the most common mistakes.
key_principles: Use potions on elites — elite rewards (relics, extra cards, gold) are worth more than saving potions
A potion used to take 0 damage from an elite is better than saving it for a boss where you'd take 10 damage anyway
Potions are free power — there is no cost to using them except opportunity cost of a better use later
You will find more potions — don't hoard them
If you have 3+ potions going into an elite, use at least 1-2
The only time to save potions is if you're about to fight a boss and your deck genuinely needs the help
potion_priority: Use offensive potions (Strength, Fire, Attack potions) on elites to kill them faster
Use defensive potions (Block, Fairy in a Bottle) when you'd otherwise take lethal or near-lethal damage
Smoke Bomb is an emergency escape — use it if a fight is going badly and you'd lose 40+ HP
Entropic Brew / Fruit Juice are best used before tough fights to maximize their value

gold_management.description: Gold is valuable but should be spent strategically. Don't hoard gold — spend it at shops on high-impact purchases.
key_principles: Card removal is almost always worth the gold — removing a Strike or Defend improves every future fight
Relics from shops can be game-changing — evaluate them against your deck's needs
Don't buy cards from shops unless they fill a critical need — card rewards are free
Save 300-400+ gold for a shop visit for maximum value
Prioritize: Card Removal > Key Relics > Potions > Cards
shop_priority: 1. Card removal (always buy at least one removal per shop visit)
2. High-synergy relics that complement your deck
3. Potions if you're about to fight an elite or boss
4. Cards only if they fill a critical gap in your deck
5. Colorless cards if they're premium (Apotheosis, Master of Strategy, etc.)

act_transitions.description: What your deck should look like at each stage of the run.

requirements: Enough frontload to kill hallway enemies in 2-3 turns
Some block generation beyond starting Defends
Deck is mostly complete — skip most card rewards
Focus on upgrades and card removal
Prepare specifically for the Act 3 boss
Ensure you have answers for the toughest fights

meta_principles.adaptability: Never force a build. Adapt to what the game offers you. The best players build around the cards and relics they find, not the archetype they wanted.
meta_principles.information_usage: Use all available information: upcoming enemies, map layout, boss identity, current HP, potion slots. Every decision should incorporate known information.
meta_principles.risk_assessment: Every decision involves risk. Calculate expected outcomes: 'If I take this elite path, I gain a relic but might lose 20 HP. Is that worth it given my current state?'
meta_principles.long_term_thinking: Don't optimize for the current fight — optimize for the current ACT. A card that's bad now but great for the boss is worth taking if you can survive without it until then.
meta_principles.practice_mindset: Every loss is a learning opportunity. Ask 'What could I have done differently?' after every run. The best players constantly self-evaluate.
